newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus talks set to start in U.S. with high hopes.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus talks set to start in U.S. with high hopes.

text.p: The two rival leaders of divided Cyprus come face to face at a rural retreat in New York state this week in an attempt to make headway in a dispute that has defied solution for decades.

Once friends but now bitter foes, Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash and Greek Cypriot leader Glafcos Clerides are meeting for the first time in almost three years at the urging of United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan at an unofficial summit.

Mediators hope the Camp David-style talks starting on Wednesday under a media blackout will kickstart negotiations on reunification and lead to lasting peace on the eastern Mediterranean island, now split by 180 km (112 miles) of barbed wire.

"We are going to New York with goodwill and in the hope that a process for reconstituting a new bi-zonal partnership state will start," said Denktash, head of a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in the northern third of Cyprus recognised only by Ankara.
"A bi-communal problem like Cyprus can only be settled by treating both sides to the problem as equals."
In the south, Foreign Minister Yiannakis Cassoulides of the internationally recognised Greek Cypriot-led government seemed equally optimistic:

"We are going with an open mind to negotiate in a positive and constructive spirit, ready for an honourable compromise. If the other side comes to the table in the same spirit, then a solution is in sight."
But the clock is ticking for Cyprus.
It is due to start talks on accession to the European Union in early 1998, a process that would be less complicated if the island were reunited.

And a year from now, the Greek Cypriots expect to take delivery of a Russian anti-aircraft missile system Turkey has vowed to destroy if deployed -- a move that would be bound to spark a response from Greece, traditionally the closest ally of the Greek Cypriots.

An artificial calm has settled on the island, but last summer Cyprus was hit by the worst violence since Turkey invaded in 1974, with a series of killings during clashes along the ceasefire line separating the two sides.

"I think one of the biggest mistakes somebody could make is to say that because the Cyprus problem has been around for decades, it is going to be around for decades more," said Gustave Feissel, resident representative in Cyprus of the U.N. Secretary-General.
"I don't think the Cyprus question will continue for many years. It will lead to a crossroads in the relative near term which will decide how things are going to go," he told Reuters recently.
"It is important for people to realise the fact that it is sunny outside does not mean everything is perfect and that things are not changing from under our feet."
Citing their rights as a guarantor power, Turkish forces invaded northern Cyprus in July 1974 after a brief Greek Cypriot coup engineered by the military then ruling Greece.
The coup collapsed but the Turkish forces remained, effectively splitting the island and heightening tension between Ankara and Athens -- a NATO partner and the second guarantor power of Cyprus.
Since then it has been impossible to reconcile the two sides on issues such as territorial concessions and constitutional and security arrangements in a federal state.
When Denktash and Clerides meet at a New York state resort called Troutbeck, they will not have a set agenda on the table.
With two advisers each and in the presence of Diego Cordovez, the U.N. Secretary-General's special adviser, and Feissel, the two leaders will negotiate for five days under a media blackout.
The arrangements are reminiscent of the talks between Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin and Egypt's President Anwar Sadat at the U.S. presidential retreat at Camp David, Maryland, in 1978.

"I think everybody understands that while the talks are going on, everybody should feel as relaxed as possible and they shouldn't have to worry that every word they utter is on TV that same evening," said Feissel.

"The only things we have set are some of the things happening on the first day. After that we are going to play it by ear. All kinds of combinations are possible... we will have joint meetings or they may decide to meet by themselves without us."
Privately, diplomats concede that scope for real progress is constrained by an expected autumn lull in the procedure for presidential elections in the Cypriot government in February.
"What we are really looking for this summer is an unofficial agreement, if you like, that is solid enough to stick until the resumption of the negotiations," said a European diplomatic source.
"Perhaps with some low-level working committees with representatives of the two sides. Something to keep things alive."
